hints: Notice the plates remain connected to the d.c. supply, so the potential difference $V$ across them is fixed while the plate separation $d$ shrinks.
Connect this to the uniform-field relation $E = V/d$ at point P, which is the same everywhere between the plates even though P stays mid-way.
Since constant speed toward each other makes $d = d_0 - ct$, sketch how $V/(d_0 - ct)$ changes - does the rise stay steady, flatten, or steepen with $t$?
walkthrough: The d.c. supply holds the plate potential difference $V$ constant, while moving together at constant speed makes separation decrease linearly: $d = d_0 - ct$ where $c$ is a positive constant.
For a uniform field the strength is the same at P as elsewhere: $E = V/d$, so position mid-way does not introduce extra variation.
Substitute the changing separation: $E(t) = V/(d_0 - ct)$ with numerator $V$ constant and denominator decreasing with $t$.
As $t$ increases the denominator gets smaller, so $E$ increases. Differentiating, $dE/dt = Vc/(d_0 - ct)^2$, which itself grows as $t$ increases, so the $E$-$t$ curve steepens.
An increasing $E$ with increasing gradient matches the rising, upward-curving graph. This is option D.

options.A: E decreases with $t$, but with $V$ fixed and separation $d$ decreasing, $E = V/d$ must increase.
options.B: E decreases with $t$, which would need increasing $d$ or decreasing $V$, opposite to plates moving together on a d.c. supply.
options.C: E increases but levels off, whereas $E = V/(d_0 - ct)$ grows faster and faster as the denominator shrinks.
options.D: E increases with an increasing gradient, matching $E = V/d$ with $V$ constant and $d$ decreasing linearly with $t$.
